title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the King Who Weeps
summary: In Jericho, Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a wealthy chief tax collector, who responds by giving half his possessions to the poor and repaying fourfold anyone he has cheated. Because the crowd expects the kingdom to appear at once, Jesus tells a parable of a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom, entrusts money to his servants, and returns to judge. He then rides into Jerusalem on a colt to the praise of his disciples, weeps over the city's coming destruction, drives the sellers out of the temple, and teaches there daily.
story:
The long road to Jerusalem that began at 9:51, when Jesus “resolutely set out for Jerusalem”, reaches its end in this chapter. Jesus has just healed a blind man as he approached Jericho (18:35-43), and Zacchaeus is the last person he meets on the way. The story gathers up Luke's great themes: the rich and the poor, tax collectors and sinners, repentance shown in the use of money, the grumbling of onlookers (5:30, 15:2), and Jesus as the one who seeks and saves the lost. It also answers the scene with the rich ruler a chapter earlier, who went away sad because he was very wealthy (18:23). The disciples then asked who could be saved, and Jesus replied, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” (18:27). Zacchaeus, also very wealthy, is the camel that passes through the needle's eye.

The parable of the minas is the last teaching on the road. Luke says Jesus told it because the crowd thought the kingdom of God would appear immediately (verse 11), and the story points instead to a king who must go away, a time of faithful work, and a return with judgment. Then the king arrives. From verse 28 onward everything happens in and around Jerusalem: the entry, the lament over the city, the temple, and the days of teaching that fill chapters 20 and 21. Verses 47 and 48 open a frame that closes at 21:37-38, where Jesus again teaches daily in the temple and all the people come to hear him. Within that frame the leaders look for a way to destroy him, and the Passover and the arrest follow in chapter 22.
historical:
Jericho in Jesus' day was not the ancient mound of Joshua 6 but a newer town a little to the south, beside the Wadi Qelt, where the Hasmonean kings and then Herod the Great built winter palaces. Ehud Netzer excavated those palaces from 1973 onward. The plain was famous for its date palms and its balsam, a costly aromatic resin (Josephus, Jewish War 4.459-475; Strabo, Geography 16.2.41), and it lay on the road from Perea across the Jordan, a natural place for tolls on goods moving between the territories of Herod Antipas and the Roman province of Judea. Herod the Great spent his last days in his Jericho palace and died there about 4 BC, and his son Archelaus rebuilt the palace magnificently (Antiquities 17.340). Zacchaeus's title, architelōnēs, ‘chief tax collector’, occurs nowhere else in the Bible. He probably held the contract for the district's tolls and employed collectors under him, which explains both his wealth and his reputation. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Zakkai, from a root meaning pure or innocent, a family name that appears among the returned exiles (Ezra 2:9, Nehemiah 7:14).

The parable of the nobleman who goes to a distant country to receive a kingdom retells recent history. Herod the Great had gone to Rome about 40 BC and been named king by the Senate. When he died, his will named Archelaus king, and Archelaus sailed to Rome to have it confirmed by Augustus, after his troops had killed about three thousand people at Passover in the temple courts (Antiquities 17.213-218). A delegation of fifty Jews followed him, joined in Rome by more than eight thousand Jews living there, and asked the emperor to free them from Herodian rule altogether (Antiquities 17.299-314; Jewish War 2.80-92). Augustus gave Archelaus half the kingdom with the lesser title of ethnarch and the promise of the crown if he proved worthy. He ruled Judea, Samaria, and Idumea so harshly that in AD 6, after complaints from both Jews and Samaritans, Augustus deposed him and banished him to Vienne in Gaul (Antiquities 17.342-344), and Judea came under Roman prefects. Matthew 2:22 mentions him. For hearers near Jericho, where Archelaus had built, the story of a nobleman, a hostile embassy, and a vengeful return needed no explanation.

The road from Jericho climbs about a thousand meters (over 3,000 feet) in some 25 kilometers (15 miles) to the Mount of Olives, where Bethphage and Bethany stood on the eastern slope. From the descent on the western side (verse 37) the whole city and the temple came suddenly into view. Forty years later the Tenth Legion camped on the Mount of Olives during the siege of AD 70 (Jewish War 5.70). Titus first raised earthworks against the walls and then, when the defenders burned them, enclosed the city with a wall of circumvallation some 39 stadia long with thirteen forts, built in three days, so that no one could get in or out (Jewish War 5.499-511). Famine followed, then the storming of the city, the burning of the temple, and the razing of Jerusalem. Josephus puts the dead at 1,100,000 and the captives at 97,000 (Jewish War 6.420), figures that are surely inflated but convey the scale. The same words Jesus uses in verse 43 also fit the Babylonian siege of 588 to 586 BC (2 Kings 25:1-4), and they echo the prophets' descriptions of it (Isaiah 29:3, Ezekiel 4:2).
cultural:
Tax collectors were ranked with thieves in popular opinion and in later Jewish law. The Mishnah allows a man to make a false vow to murderers, robbers, and tax collectors to save his goods (m. Nedarim 3:4) and forbids taking change from a customs collector's chest (m. Bava Kamma 10:1). The verb Zacchaeus uses, sukophanteō (verse 8), means to extort by intimidation or false accusation; the only other New Testament use is John the Baptist's warning to soldiers (3:14). His promise measures itself against the Law. Ordinary restitution for goods taken by fraud was the full amount plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5, Numbers 5:7). Fourfold was the penalty for a stolen sheep that had been slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1, which is 21:37 in the Hebrew Bible), the penalty David pronounced on the rich man of Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:6). Roman law also set a fourfold penalty for theft caught in the act (Gaius, Institutes 3.189). Giving half his property to the poor went further still: a later rabbinic ruling advised that a man should not give away more than a fifth, lest he become poor himself (b. Ketubot 50a).

The tree Zacchaeus climbs is the sycamore-fig (Ficus sycomorus), a lowland tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb and common around Jericho; Amos tended them (Amos 7:14) and Solomon made cedar as common as sycamores (1 Kings 10:27). A wealthy official running ahead and climbing a tree made a public spectacle of himself. Jesus answers with a public honor: he names Zacchaeus and invites himself as a guest, and in a culture where sharing a table meant accepting someone, the crowd hears that as endorsement of a sinner (verse 7).

A mina was a weight of silver equal to a hundred drachmas, roughly a hundred days' wages for a laborer; sixty minas made a talent. The nobleman gives each servant one mina, a modest sum, and rewards faithfulness with cities, the way client kings gave loyal servants towns to govern. Tying money in a cloth was considered careless: the Mishnah holds a man liable who took a deposit, tied it up, and slung it behind him (m. Bava Metzia 3:10), and the Talmud adds that money is safely kept only in the ground (b. Bava Metzia 42a). The bank (trapeza, literally ‘table’) was the money-changer's or lender's table where deposits could earn interest. The Law forbade Israelites to charge interest to one another but not to foreigners (Deuteronomy 23:19-20), and deposit banking was common in the Greek and Roman world.

The entry follows royal custom. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose (Numbers 19:2, 1 Samuel 6:7), and David had Solomon ride his own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33). Spreading garments on the road was homage to a new king (2 Kings 9:13). Luke leaves out the palm branches and the Hebrew cry Hosanna, perhaps because his Greek readers would not have understood them, and gives the acclamation of Psalm 118:26, the psalm pilgrims sang at the feasts, with the word King added. The market in the temple's outer court sold animals for sacrifice and changed money for the temple tax; Mark describes it more fully (Mark 11:15-17).
literary:
The chapter closes one section of the Gospel and opens another. Luke's road to Jerusalem (9:51-19:27) ends with a story and a parable, and verse 28, “He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem”, begins the section of teaching in the city (19:28-21:38). The Zacchaeus story is built on seeing and seeking: Zacchaeus seeks to see who Jesus is (verse 3), climbs to see him (verse 4), and is seen first, as Jesus looks up and calls him by name (verse 5). The same verb, zēteō, returns in verse 10, where the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Verses 9 and 10 are a pronouncement that turns a local scene into a summary of Jesus' whole mission, and the word “today” (verses 5 and 9) links it to the angels' announcement (2:11), the sermon at Nazareth (4:21), and the promise to the dying criminal (23:43).

The parable weaves two plots. In one, a master entrusts money to servants and returns to settle accounts, the plot Matthew tells as the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30). In the other, a nobleman seeks a kingdom, his citizens reject him, and he returns to punish them, a plot found only in Luke. Many interpreters, among them Joachim Jeremias in The Parables of Jesus, think Luke or his source combined two stories; others think Jesus told a single composite parable. Either way, the joined plots let the parable address two audiences at once: disciples who must be faithful in the king's absence, and a city about to reject its king. The third servant's excuse is answered out of his own mouth (verse 22), a pattern of judgment by one's own words.

The entry is told with command and fulfillment (verses 30-34), as in the preparation of the Passover (22:8-13). Luke's crowd is not a general crowd but “the whole multitude of disciples” praising God for the miracles they had seen (verse 37), and their cry, peace in heaven and glory in the highest, echoes the angels' song at the birth (2:14), where peace was on earth. The Pharisees' objection and Jesus' answer about the stones (verses 39-40) are found only in Luke. The lament (verses 41-44), also only in Luke, is a prophetic oracle of judgment in the classic form: a lament, an accusation, and a sentence introduced by ‘days will come’, ending with the reason. It echoes Jeremiah, who wept for his people (Jeremiah 9:1), and it looks back to Jesus' earlier lament that Jerusalem's house would be left desolate (13:34-35). Luke tells the temple action in two verses and then frames the next three chapters with a notice of daily teaching (19:47-48, 21:37-38) that sets the people, who hang on his words, against the leaders, who are seeking to kill him.

outline.t: The parable of the ten minas
Jesus clears the temple and teaches daily

doctrines.note: Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house”, and states the purpose of his whole mission: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” The initiative is his: he sees, calls, and invites himself before Zacchaeus says a word. Zacchaeus's generosity is the fruit of that welcome, not its price.

Zacchaeus never uses the word repent, but his response is repentance in the concrete form John the Baptist asked of tax collectors (3:12-13): restitution beyond what the Law required and generosity to the poor. Whether his words are a resolve or a description of his habit is debated (see the interpretation section), but either way Jesus names the result salvation.

Luke sets a rich man who is saved beside a rich ruler who went away sad (18:18-27). Zacchaeus does not give away everything, but money no longer holds him. In the parable, the king entrusts money to servants and asks what they did with it, so that possessions become a stewardship for which disciples will give account.

The parable corrects the expectation that the kingdom would appear at once (verse 11). The king goes to a distant country to receive his kingdom and returns to call his servants to account, a picture Luke's readers would connect with Jesus' ascension and his promised return (Acts 1:9-11). The time between is for faithful work, not idle waiting.

The citizens who refuse the king's rule are judged (verse 27), and Jesus announces the destruction of Jerusalem because it did not recognize the time of its visitation (verse 44). Yet the one who announces judgment weeps as he does it. In this chapter judgment is real, rooted in the rejection of God's king, and grieved by that king.

words.note: Sēmeron, today. It occurs about 41 times in the New Testament and 11 in Luke, more than in any other Gospel, twice in this story (verses 5 and 9). In Luke the word marks the moment when God's salvation arrives in a person's life: the Savior born today (2:11), Scripture fulfilled today (4:21), and the promise to the criminal on the cross, today you will be with me (23:43). Salvation in Luke is not only a future hope but a present visit.

Sukophanteō, to extort, to cheat by intimidation or false accusation. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke: John the Baptist's instruction to soldiers not to extort (3:14) and Zacchaeus's promise here (verse 8). In classical Greek a sukophantēs was a blackmailing informer. The ‘if’ clause is a Greek condition that presents the case as real; Zacchaeus is not denying that he cheated but promising to repay whatever he took that way.

Sōtēria, salvation, deliverance. It occurs about 49 times in the New Testament and five times in Luke, three of them in Zechariah's song (1:69, 1:71, 1:77). BDAG gives both rescue from danger and the salvation God brings. Luke uses it for the long-promised deliverance of God's people, and verse 9 says it has arrived in a tax collector's house because this man too is a son of Abraham.

Apollumi, to destroy, perish, or in the perfect active participle, to be lost. It occurs about ninety times in the New Testament and 27 in Luke, eight of them in the three parables of the lost in chapter 15. The phrase in verse 10, to apolōlos, ‘that which was lost’, is the phrase of Ezekiel 34:16 in the Greek Old Testament, where God promises to seek the lost sheep his shepherds had neglected. The same verb appears in verse 47, where the leaders seek to destroy Jesus.

Mna, the mina, a weight of silver worth a hundred drachmas. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, all in this parable. Each servant receives the same small sum, and what distinguishes them is what they did with it. Matthew's parable uses the talent, sixty times as much and given in different amounts; Luke's version stresses faithfulness in a very small matter (verse 17, compare 16:10).

Eirēnē, peace. It occurs about 91 times in the New Testament and 14 in Luke, twice in this chapter. The disciples cry peace in heaven (verse 38), and Jesus laments that Jerusalem did not know what would bring it peace (verse 42). In the Greek Old Testament eirēnē translates shalom, wholeness and well-being under God's rule, and Luke has used it since Zechariah's song of the Dawn who guides our feet into the way of peace (1:79). There may be a play on the city's name, often explained as ‘city of peace’.

Klaiō, to weep aloud, to wail. It occurs about 40 times in the New Testament and 11 in Luke. Verse 41 is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus is said to weep with this verb; John 11:35 uses another, dakruō, for his tears at Lazarus's tomb. Klaiō is the loud weeping of mourning, used of the women on the way to the cross, whom Jesus tells to weep for themselves and their children (23:28), words that return to the fate of the city lamented here.

Episkopē, visitation, oversight, and later the office of an overseer or bishop (Acts 1:20, 1 Timothy 3:1). It occurs four times in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew pequddah, the time when God visits his people in rescue or in judgment, and the phrase ‘time of visitation’ comes from the prophets (Jeremiah 6:15 in the Greek). Luke has used the related verb for God visiting and redeeming his people (1:68, 1:78, 7:16). Jesus' coming was that visit, and the city did not recognize it.

christ:
In this chapter Jesus acts openly as the king Israel had been promised, and Luke shows what kind of king he is. He comes first to a despised tax collector and states the purpose of his coming in words that recall God's promise in Ezekiel 34: after the shepherds of Israel had failed, God said he would himself search for his flock and seek them out (Ezekiel 34:11, 34:16). When Jesus says that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, he takes up the role God claimed for himself.

The parable tells the reader that his kingdom will not appear in the way the crowd expects. The king must go to a distant country to receive it. Luke's readers knew where Jesus went: through the cross and resurrection to the right hand of God, where, as Peter says, God made him both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:33-36). Daniel's vision had shown the Son of Man coming to the Ancient of Days to receive dominion, glory, and kingship (Daniel 7:13-14), and Luke will end with Jesus taken up in a cloud and the promise that he will come back in the same way (Acts 1:9-11). The parable's servants are disciples who must work in his absence, and its citizens are those who say, “We do not want this man to rule over us.”

Then the king enters his city. He rides a colt, as Zechariah said Zion's king would come, “humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt” (Zechariah 9:9). His disciples greet him with the pilgrim blessing of Psalm 118, adding the title King. When the Pharisees ask him to silence them, he answers that the stones would cry out, a claim that creation itself knows who he is. Yet this king weeps over the city that will reject him. The visitation it missed was God's own visit (1:68), and Jesus grieves over Jerusalem as the prophets did and as God does in the prophets. He enters the temple and calls it “My house”, the words of Isaiah 56:7 in which God speaks, and he stays there teaching until the hour of darkness comes (22:53). The weeping king of this chapter is the crucified king of chapter 23, whose title is nailed above his head, and the risen king who opens the Scriptures to show that the Christ had to suffer and then enter his glory (24:26).
interpretation:
Early readers were curious about Zacchaeus himself. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 4.6.35) reports that some identified him with Matthias, the apostle chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1:26), and the Apostolic Constitutions (7.46), a fourth-century church order, name Zacchaeus the tax collector as the first bishop of Caesarea. Neither tradition can be tested. Ambrose of Milan, in his Exposition of Luke, and Augustine, in his Sermon 174, made much of the sycamore, whose name suggested to them a ‘foolish fig’: Zacchaeus was willing to look foolish to see Jesus, and Augustine urged his hearers not to be ashamed to climb the tree of the cross. In the medieval West the story became the Gospel for the dedication of a church, whose Mass opens with Terribilis est locus iste (Genesis 28:17), because salvation came to a house. The Orthodox churches read it on Zacchaeus Sunday, the Sunday before the Triodion that prepares for Lent, and the Revised Common Lectionary (Proper 26) and the Roman lectionary (Thirty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time) read it in Year C. A modern debate turns on the present tenses of verse 8. Joseph Fitzmyer (Anchor Bible, 1985) and Alan Mitchell (Biblica, 1990) read them as customary: Zacchaeus defends himself, and Jesus vindicates a man the crowd had misjudged. Dennis Hamm (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1988) and most commentators read them as a resolve made in response to Jesus, and so as a conversion story.

The parable of the minas has a tangled history. Eusebius (Theophany) reports a Jewish-Christian gospel in which one servant multiplied the money, one hid it and was only rebuked, and one squandered it on harlots and was imprisoned. Most readers from the fathers to the Reformers took the nobleman as Christ, his departure as the ascension, and the minas as gifts to be used for God, and Calvin expounded it alongside Matthew's talents in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555). Luke Timothy Johnson (Novum Testamentum, 1982) argued that it is not about delay at all: Jesus receives his kingship in the events that follow, as the entry immediately shows, and the enemies' fate points to Jerusalem. Richard Rohrbaugh (Biblical Theology Bulletin, 1993) read it from the side of ancient peasants, for whom a master who reaps where he did not sow would be the villain and the third servant the honest man, a reading that others judge to fit poorly with Luke's framing.

The lament over Jerusalem has had a sobering life in the liturgy. In the Lutheran churches, Luke 19:41-48 was the Gospel for the Tenth Sunday after Trinity, and after Johannes Bugenhagen published a German account of the destruction of Jerusalem drawn from Josephus in 1534, it became customary in many places to read that history at vespers that day, which came to be called the Judensonntag. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote three cantatas for the day, Schauet doch und sehet (BWV 46, 1723), Nimm von uns, Herr, du treuer Gott (BWV 101, 1724), and Herr, deine Augen sehen nach dem Glauben (BWV 102, 1726). The day often framed the destruction as God's punishment of the Jews, a use most churches now repudiate, and many now read the passage as a warning to the church itself. On the western slope of the Mount of Olives, the Franciscan church of Dominus Flevit, ‘the Lord wept’, designed by Antonio Barluzzi and built in 1955 over remains of an older chapel, has a teardrop-shaped dome and a window looking across to the city. Enrique Simonet's large painting Flevit super illam (1892), now in the Prado, shows the same view. Verses 28 to 40 are the Gospel of the Liturgy of the Palms in the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C.
text:
English Bibles differ at a few points in this chapter, mostly where the King James Version follows later manuscripts. In verse 13 the King James Version's ‘Occupy till I come’ follows the Textus Receptus, which reads heōs, ‘until’, and uses ‘occupy’ in its older sense of doing business. The earliest manuscripts read en hō erchomai, ‘while I am coming’, and Westcott and Hort print the verb as an infinitive, ‘to do business’, rather than a command. The meaning is the same: trade with the money during the master's absence.

In verse 45 later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add ‘and them that bought’ to those Jesus drove out, harmonizing with Mark 11:15 and Matthew 21:12; the earliest manuscripts have only those who were selling. In verse 46 the King James Version reads ‘My house is the house of prayer’, while the critical texts read the future ‘will be’, matching Isaiah 56:7. In every manuscript Luke's quotation of Isaiah 56:7 lacks the words ‘for all the nations’, which Mark keeps (Mark 11:17). Some think Luke omitted them because the temple had already fallen when he wrote and could no longer become that house; others think he simply shortened the quotation, as he often does, and that the nations' access to God is for him a theme of Acts rather than of the temple.

teach.big: Jesus comes as the king who seeks the lost, entrusts his servants with his goods until he returns, and weeps over those who refuse him, so that the only fitting responses are glad welcome, faithful work, and recognition of God's visit while it is today.

outline.t: A rich man with a bad name wants to see Jesus and will look foolish to do it; curiosity is where Luke's great conversions often begin.
Jesus sees him first, calls him by name, and must stay at his house; grace takes the initiative and scandalizes the respectable.
Salvation shows itself in the wallet: restitution beyond the Law and generosity to the poor are the fruit of being found, and the Son of Man came for exactly such people.
The kingdom does not arrive on the crowd's timetable: the king must go away to receive it, and not everyone wants him to reign.
Faithfulness in small things is what the returning king rewards, and his reward is more responsibility, not retirement.
The servant who hid his mina was paralyzed by a false picture of his master; what we believe about God shapes what we do with his gifts.
Refusing the king's rule is not a neutral choice; the parable ends with a warning that Luke's readers would soon see played out in Jerusalem.
Jesus arranges his own entry as the humble king of Zechariah 9:9, and his disciples give him the homage due a king.
The disciples praise God for what they have seen, and Jesus refuses to silence them; if people will not confess the king, creation will.
The king weeps over the city that will reject him; judgment is real, and it grieves the one who announces it.
Jesus reclaims God's house for prayer and teaches there daily; the people hang on his words while the leaders plot his death.

teach.pitfalls:
The Zacchaeus story is often taught to children as a story about being short, and to adults as a story about seeking Jesus. Luke's emphasis falls on Jesus seeking Zacchaeus (verse 10) and on what salvation did to his money. Preachers should resist making the restitution the condition of salvation (Jesus invited himself first) and also resist spiritualizing it away: in Luke, repentance that does not reach the purse is suspect (3:10-14, 18:22).

The parable of the minas is frequently preached as a lesson in using one's natural abilities, because the English word ‘talent’ came to mean a gift from Matthew's parable. Luke's parable is about faithfulness to an absent king with what he has entrusted, and the minas are his, not ours. It is also misused as an endorsement of investment returns or free-market economics, or, in the opposite direction, flattened into a story in which the nobleman is simply Archelaus and the third servant a hero. Neither reading attends to Luke's framing in verse 11 or to the entry that follows. Do not identify every feature of the nobleman with Jesus: parables can use hard human figures to make a point about God by comparison, as the unjust judge does in 18:1-8.

The lament must not be preached as God's rejection of the Jewish people. Jesus weeps as a Jew over his own city, in the line of Jeremiah, and the Jewish crowds in this chapter hang on his words (verse 48). The church's long habit of using this passage against Jews, including the Judensonntag, is a warning about how the text can be abused. Finally, Palm Sunday preaching that says the same crowd cheered on Sunday and shouted crucify on Friday goes beyond Luke, who says the praise came from the multitude of disciples.
teach.pastoral: Zacchaeus will speak to people who carry shame about money: debts they caused, business dealings they regret, family members they cheated. The story offers them a welcome that comes before restitution and a path of repair that follows it. Some listeners have been financially exploited, and they need to hear that Jesus' welcome of Zacchaeus included a reckoning with those he had wronged. The third servant's fear (verse 21) will press on the scrupulous, who see God as a harsh master and are frozen by fear of failure; the parable shows that fear distorts, not that God is harsh. The weeping king speaks to anyone grieving a place or a people that has turned away, and to those who fear that God only condemns. He grieves before he judges.

hard.q: The king in the parable orders his enemies slain before him. Does this describe how Jesus will treat those who reject him?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and has been pressed from several sides. If the nobleman stands for Jesus, as most interpreters from the fathers onward have assumed, then Jesus portrays himself as a king who has his opponents executed in his presence, and verse 27 has been used in Christian history to justify violence against unbelievers and against Jews in particular. Readers such as Richard Rohrbaugh (Biblical Theology Bulletin, 1993) argue from the other direction that a greedy, harsh nobleman who reaps where he did not sow and slaughters his opponents cannot be meant as a picture of God or Christ at all, and that Jesus' first hearers would have recognized Archelaus and sided with the victims. On this reading the traditional allegory has made Jesus the likeness of a tyrant.

The responses start with the nature of parables. Jesus often argues from the lesser to the greater or by contrast, using figures whose conduct is plainly not God's: an unjust judge (18:1-8), a dishonest manager (16:1-8), a man who will not get out of bed (11:5-8). The point of comparison here is not the nobleman's character but the structure of the story: a king goes away to receive a kingdom, his servants are accountable, and those who refuse his rule face the consequences of that refusal. Most modern commentators read the parable on those lines. Luke Timothy Johnson (Novum Testamentum, 1982) and others connect verse 27 directly with the lament a few verses later: the city that refuses its king will be surrounded and leveled, not by Jesus' command but as the historical consequence Jesus foresees and grieves. Others take it more broadly as the final judgment, which the New Testament does attribute to Christ (Acts 10:42, 17:31). What no reading can do is turn the verse into a warrant for Christians to punish unbelievers; Jesus rebuked his disciples for wanting to call down fire on a Samaritan village (9:54-55), and Luke sets beside this verse the image of the king weeping over his enemies' city. Readers may disagree about how closely the nobleman mirrors Jesus, but the chapter's own portrait of the king is the one who seeks the lost and weeps over the lost.

hard.q: Do verses 43 and 44 describe the siege of AD 70 so exactly that Luke must have written after it?
hard.a:
Many scholars think so. The prediction speaks of enemies throwing up a barricade (charax), surrounding the city, hemming it in on every side, leveling it with its children, and leaving no stone on another, and Titus did build a siege wall around Jerusalem, starve it, and raze it (Josephus, Jewish War 5.499-511, 7.1-3). Read with 21:20, where Luke has ‘Jerusalem surrounded by armies’ in place of Mark's ‘abomination of desolation’, the passage looks to the majority of critical scholars, including Joseph Fitzmyer and Raymond Brown, like a prediction sharpened by knowledge of the event, and it is one of their main reasons for dating Luke between about AD 75 and 90. Skeptical readers go further and treat any detailed prediction as written after the fact, on the principle that the historian cannot appeal to foreknowledge.

Other scholars answer that the wording is not specific to AD 70. C. H. Dodd argued in The Fall of Jerusalem and the ‘Abomination of Desolation’ (Journal of Roman Studies, 1947) that Luke's language in 19:42-44 and 21:20-24 is drawn from the Greek Old Testament's accounts of the Babylonian capture of Jerusalem and contains none of the features, such as the burning of the temple, the factions inside the walls, or the famine, that only the Roman siege would suggest. The phrases can be traced: the barricade and encirclement in Isaiah 29:3 and Ezekiel 4:2, and children dashed to the ground in the Greek of Hosea 10:14 and Psalm 137:9. Ancient sieges followed a common pattern, and any prophet who foresaw one would describe it in these terms. John A. T. Robinson (Redating the New Testament, 1976) built on Dodd in arguing for dates before AD 70, and defenders of an early date note that Acts, written after Luke, never mentions the city's fall. It is also widely agreed, by scholars as different as E. P. Sanders and N. T. Wright, that Jesus did speak of the temple's destruction, and Josephus reports that another Jesus, son of Ananias, cried woe against Jerusalem from AD 62 until the siege (Jewish War 6.300-309). A prediction of the city's fall was not unthinkable before it happened.

The evidence of these verses alone cannot settle the date, which depends on the whole case set out in the introduction to Luke. What the text itself stresses is not the accuracy of the forecast but its cause, the city's failure to recognize God's visit, and its tone, which is grief.
